L141: Spec: 【64†`specs/dims-disambiguate.md`】. Spec-only for now; the implementation follows on this branch once the spec is approved. `/analyze-spec` ran (ambiguity 9.5%).
L142: ## The problem
L143: 
L144: When you read a dims value in `atlas-trace` or the prover today, you can't tell whether it's the model's real shape or its power-of-two padded shape. It depends on how the model was compiled:
L145:   * With padding (the importer, so every real model), `pad_graph` overwrites each node's `output_dims` with padded dims, and `apply_padding` rewrites some op fields (Reshape/Broadcast `shape`) to padded values too.
L146:   * Without padding (`ModelBuilder::build()`, so most unit tests), the same fields hold the real dims.
L147: 
L148: So the same field means two different things depending on the caller, and nothing in its name says which. Some symptoms:
L149:   * The reshape protocol's `input_raw_dims` / `output_raw_dims` hold padded dims on every real model.
L150:   * `MeanOfSquares` carries both `count` and `padded_count`; the model keeps a separate `IoDims` copy of the boundary shapes. These exist only because the real dims got overwritten.
L151:   * The pow2 derivation is written in several places.
L152:   * It has already caused a soundness-relevant bug (【65†Fix padded reshape layout at the source instead of lowering it #378】: the prover read padded tensor dims where the verifier used raw ones).
L153: ## The proposal
L154: 
L155: Store the real (raw) dims everywhere; compute padded dims when needed, in one place.
L156: 
L157: Raw is the right source of truth because the mapping only goes one way: you can always get padded from raw (`next_power_of_two` per axis), but you can't get raw back from padded (5, 6, 7 and 8 all pad to 8).
L158: 
L159: Concretely:
L160:   * Nodes and op fields keep their raw dims after compile.
L161:   * The model knows, once, whether its tensors are physically padded. `physical_dims(node)` answers "what shape is the actual tensor".
L162:   * Every prover/verifier read says explicitly whether it wants raw or physical dims.
L163:   * The importer no longer needs to know padding exists.
L164: ## What doesn't change
L165:   * Tensors stay physically padded. This is about what we store, not the memory layout.
L166:   * Proofs stay byte-identical. A temporary test pins the proof hash of every checked-in zoo model from `main`; every commit must keep it green, and a follow-up PR removes it. Real GPT-2 / Dory gets a manual before/after run, reported here.
L167:   * No performance change, since the proving work is the same.
L168:   * No bug fixes, even if we find some: anything found is pinned as a `known_gap_*` test for a later PR.
L169: ## One deliberate exception
L170: 
L171: `SoftmaxLastAxis.active_len` (the real width of a padded softmax row) stays as it is. To compute it, the op's `eval` would need the node's raw input width, and `eval` only receives the padded tensors. Fixing that means changing the `eval` API (or dropping physical padding), which belongs in its own PR.
L172: ## Where review is most useful
L173:   * Is "raw stored, padded derived" the right rule? The alternative is keeping both side by side, which is roughly today's design.
L174:   * Plain `Vec<usize>` plus a model-wide layout flag, rather than `Raw`/`Padded` newtypes. Newtypes would catch mix-ups at compile time but touch every op field and every read site; the spec argues one explicit accessor is enough.
L175:   * The commit plan (spec § Execution): first route every dims read through one deliberately ambiguous accessor, then split it per call site. The goal is that every raw-vs-padded decision is visible in a single diff.

L149: Spec-only PR: `specs/adoption-program.md`, plus `docs/upstream-inventory.md` as its factual basis. It supersedes closed 【64†#396】 (program portions), 【65†#397】 and 【66†#399】, and the unopened expression-engine draft. Those four documents depended on each other in a loop, so one spec now owns the order of operations. 【66†#399】's verifier-boundary spec is stage 1 here.
L150: End state: `joltworks` is replaced by vendored, rev-pinned upstream a16z/jolt crates plus named atlas-only crates. Every algebraic op is a symbolic relation bound to its `atlas_trace` op type, with no hand-written verifier. `jolt-atlas-verifier` holds all verification. Fp128 + Akita is the only field and PCS; BN254, Dory, HyperKZG and `zk` are gone.
L151: 
L152: Order: nine stages (0–8), one PR each. Hard dependencies force the order:
L153:   * the field comes before everything;
L154:   * transcript, sumcheck and poly come before `jolt-claims`;
L155:   * `jolt-claims` comes before relations;
L156:   * `jolt-akita` needs `jolt-claims`;
L157:   * relations come before the verifier-crate moves they unblock.
L158: 
L159: Stages 0 (prerequisites, `zk` deletion) and 1 (verifier boundary) can start now.
L160: 
L161: Decisions recorded for review:
L162:   * Stage 1 has no protocol change, and that is checked across stages. A digest harness pins proof-byte and final-transcript hashes per zoo model. It is the first commit of stage 1, green on the untouched tree. Every stage declares itself behavior-preserving or protocol-breaking; only 3 (transcript) and 7a (Akita) re-pin.
L163:   * Stage 2 moves the BN254 scalar to upstream `jolt_field::Fr`, with HyperKZG and Dory converting at the `CommitmentScheme::Field` boundary. This is throwaway work that 7b deletes. It is still needed because upstream `jolt-poly` and `jolt-transcript` accept only `jolt_field` types, so stages 3–6 would otherwise have no backend with a PCS to run on.
L164:   * Stage 5 decides `jolt-claims` adoption with a two-week spike.
L165:     * Pass bar: the Mul pilot proves and verifies through the adopted claim system on a probe model, and three stress flows work (node-indexed opening, multi-consumer reduction, deferred batch).
L166:     * If it fails, the fallback is taken without further debate.
L167:     * Pilot migrations keep the existing input claim, opening points and append order, so digests reproduce.
L168:   * Stage 6: softmax's outcome follows a stated rule tied to whether 【67†restructure softmax prover to avoid sending aux vectors #218】 has merged. The closing PR checks that every op in the op-surface table has a recorded outcome.
L169:   * Stage 7a may land in parallel with stage 6. All gates switch to the default backend at that point: Akita digests, the Akita heavy job and the Akita benchmark baseline.
L170:   * Stage 7b's BN254-removal check runs on the resolved dependency graph: no `ark-bn254`/`ark-ec` with BN254 features off. Whole-crate vendoring keeps upstream's disabled BN254 features in `third_party/`.
L171:   * "Prover-free" is checked at crate level (the isolation build). At item level it uses an enumerated clippy disallow-list of prover functions and types, plus a check that rejects `::prover`/`::witness` import paths.
L172:   * Performance gate for behavior-preserving stages: the median of 3 `prove` runs on GPT-2 must be within +3% of `main`. That is Dory until 7a lands, Akita after.
L173:   * zk is deleted at stage 0 (57 pre-existing compile errors). Lattice zk is a separate in-house effort that builds on the end state.
L174: Per CONTRIBUTING, `/analyze-spec` ran on the current text: final ambiguity is 9.6%, all dimensions ≥ 0.9. It added the performance gate and the per-stage behavior classes. The four Copilot findings from the last review round are addressed in 【68†`71a9dff`】.

L212: ### Scope of Contributions
L213: 
L214: The contributions in [1]-[4] are relevant for the following scope of applications:
L215:   * Matrix multiplication and deep learning inference: The proposed systolic array hardware architectures from [1]-[4] improve dense matrix multiplication acceleration in general, and therefore can also be exploited in accelerator systems for accelerating all DNN models/layers that can mainly decompose to matrix multiplication, including fully-connected layers, CNNs, RNNs, and attention layers/transformer models.
L216:   * Fixed-point data types, same numerical stability: Most of the contributions focus on fixed-point data types and quantized neural network inference. It may be possible to extend some of the fixed-point concepts to floating point in future work. Additionally, since they use fixed-point data types, the presented algorithms/hardware architectures produce identical output as conventional algorithms/architectures and cause no changes to numerical stability.
L217:   * FPGA and ASIC: Results were validated on FPGA, but the proposed architectures are general and most improvements are applicable to both custom integrated circuit and FPGA implementations
L218:   * Systolic arrays, seamless system integration: The proposed architectures are systolic arrays, which are an efficient type of design for GEMM & deep learning acceleration (e.g., the Google TPU). It may also be possible to extend some of the concepts to non-systolic array designs in future work. Additionally, they increase performance-per-area but have otherwise identical functionality and interfaces as traditional systolic arrays.
L219: I.e., the algebraic enhancements are fully self-contained within the systolic arrays and do not require additional pre or post-processing steps. This means they can be easily/seamlessly swapped with traditional systolic arrays in existing accelerator systems to increase performance per MAC unit with little or no other changes required in the rest of the system and no hidden tradeoffs.
L220: ### Results Preview
L221: 
L222: Synthesis and performance results when combining the architectures from [1] and [3] compared to state-of-the-art accelerators implemented on similar compute platforms achieved up to 3× faster CNN inference, 2× higher mults/multiplier/clock cycle, and >40% higher clock frequency:
L223:

L226: #
L227: ### Accelerator System Overview
L228: The following diagram shows the deep learning accelerator system implemented in this source code used to host and validate the systolic arrays proposed in [1]-[4]. The system implementation is specialized for performing inference of non-sparse DNN models with fixed-point/quantized inputs consisting of convolutional layers, fully-connected layers, and pooling layers.
L229: All DNN layers are fully accelerated in hardware and it can accelerate ML models with arbitrary layer dimensions/kernel sizes all on a single hardware design. Input bitwidths and systolic array dimensions are parametrizable. The system is also a highly-optimized GEMM accelerator in general.
L230: System Block Diagram Overview:
L231:   * Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) / systolic array
L232:     * Contains a systolic array architecture for performing matrix multiplication
L233:     * For each method in [1]-[4], different proposed systolic arrays/MXUs are swapped for the MXU in the above system figure
L234:   * GEMM Unit
L235:     * Contains the MXU as well as SRAM and addition logic for accumulating matrix tiles to allow GEMM execution of arbitrarily-sized matrices
L236:   * Post-GEMM Unit
L237:     * Contains neural network-specific functions to be performed on the matrix multiplication outputs. This includes adding the bias values, inter-layer rescaling for quantization, activation, padding, and pooling.
L238:   * Memory Unit
L239:     * Contains memory access control logic and on-chip SRAM memory for holding layer activations
L240:     * Implements efficient caching & memory access HW algorithms, mapping convolution to GEMM in-place without data duplication/delay
L241:     * Uses memory partitioning schemes allowing SRAM memory and control to run at half or quarter clock rate while outputting new data at full clock rate, to improve overall system frequency and power
L242:   * Off-chip DDR DRAM memory for weights
L243:   * RxTx Unit
L244:     * PCIe interface to host
L245:   * Instruction Unit
L246:     * For decoding accelerator instructions sent from the host that allow the system to accelerate ML models with arbitrary layer dimensions/kernel sizes all on a single hardware design

L248: ### Source Code Overview
L249:   * compiler
L250:     * A compiler for parsing Python ML model descriptions into accelerator instructions that allow it to accelerate ML models with arbitrary layer dimensions/kernel sizes. This part also includes code for interfacing with a PCIe driver for initiating model execution on the accelerator, reading back results and performance counters, and testing the correctness of the results
L251:   * rtl
L252:     * Synthesizable SystemVerilog accelerator RTL
L253:   * sim
L254:     * Scripts for setting up simulation environments for verification
L255:   * tests
L256:     * UVM testbench source code for verifying the accelerator in simulation, written in Python and cocotb
L257:   * utils
L258:     * Additional Python packages and scripts used in this project created for general development utilities and aids
L259: The files rtl/top/define.svh and rtl/top/pkg.sv contain a number of configurable parameters such as FIP_METHOD in define.svh which defines the systolic array type (e.g., baseline, FIP, or FFIP [1]), SZI and SZJ which define the systolic array height/width, and LAYERIO_WIDTH/WEIGHT_WIDTH which define the input bitwidths.
L260: The directory rtl/arith includes mxu.sv and mac_array.sv which contain the RTL for the baseline and some of the proposed systolic array architectures (FIP and FFIP [1]) depending on the value of the parameter FIP_METHOD.
